2.6.1. The Chapter on Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
There the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
“Monks, these two extremes should not be pursued by one who has gone forth.
Which two?”
The pursuit of sensual pleasure among sense-objects, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial;

and the pursuit of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial—having avoided both these extremes, monks, the Middle Way has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; it produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
And what, monks, is that middle way realized by the Tathāgata, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
"This indeed, monks, is that Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
And this, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering:

birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, and not to obtain what one desires is also suffering."

In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. Now, monks, this is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: it is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; that is to say: [The remainder of the passage follows: ...craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation without remainder of that very craving, its relinquishing, renouncing, liberation, and detachment from it. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. And what, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. Monks, these four noble truths have been realized by me, fully understood, penetrated, mastered, and well-penetrated with wisdom. It is because I have realized these four noble truths, fully understood them, penetrated them, mastered them, and well-penetrated them with wisdom, that I claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. And this exalted knowledge and vision of mine regarding these four noble truths as they really are has become stable, attained to immovability, enriched, and brought to fulfillment in this very life. Monks, so long as this exalted knowledge and vision of mine regarding these four noble truths as they really are was not stable, attained to immovability, enriched, and brought to fulfillment in this very life, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. Craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
Now, monks, this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering:
it is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, its abandonment, its release, and its non-attachment.
And this, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering:
it is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say, right view ...
[and so on] ... right concentration.
“‘This is the noble truth of suffering,’ monks—regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true insight, and light.
‘That this noble truth of suffering must be fully understood’—regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true insight, and light.
‘That this noble truth of suffering has been fully understood’—regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true insight, and light.”

“‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’— regarding these things unheard before, vision arose in me, bhikkhus, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, and light arose. ‘But this noble truth of the origin of suffering must be abandoned’— regarding these things unheard before, bhikkhus … [as above] … ‘It has been abandoned’—
regarding these things unheard before, bhikkhus, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, and light arose.”
“‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’—regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in me, bhikkhus, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.

‘That this noble truth of the cessation of suffering must be realized’—regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in me, bhikkhus, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized’—regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in me, bhikkhus, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.”
‘This is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering’— thus, monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true insight, and light.

‘That noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering must be developed’— thus, monks …pe… ‘That noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed’—
thus, monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true insight, and light.
“Monks, as long as my knowledge and vision regarding these four noble truths— thus in their three rounds and twelve aspects—
was not perfectly purified as they really are, so long, monks, did I not declare among the generation with its devas,
Māras, and Brahmās, among this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, that I had attained the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.”
“I have awakened,” I declared. But when, monks,
my knowledge and vision regarding these four noble truths— having three rounds and twelve aspects—
had become perfectly purified as they really are, then, monks, in this world with its devas, Māras, and...
“In this world with its brahmās, its recluses and brahmins, its generation with its devas and humans, I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And the knowledge and vision arose in me:
‘My liberation is unshakable; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.’”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The group of five monks were uplifted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the dustless, stainless Dharma-eye arose in the Venerable Koṇḍañña.
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
And when the Wheel of Dhamma had been set in motion by the Blessed One, the earth-dwelling deities raised a cry:

“This unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by the Blessed One at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana; it cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, by any god, Māra, or Brahmā, nor by anyone in the world.”
Having heard the sound of the earth-dwelling deities, the deities of the Four Great Kings raised a cry;
having heard the sound of the deities of the Four Great Kings, the Tāvatiṃsa deities...
[and so on] ...the Yāma deities... [and so on].
the Tusita devas …pe… the Nimmānarati devas …pe… the Paranimmitavasavatti devas …pe…
The gods of the Brahma-world raised a cry:

"This unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion by the Blessed One at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana—a wheel that cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, by any god, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone in the world.
Thus, at that very moment, at that very instant, at that very second, the sound rose up as far as the Brahma-world.
And this ten-thousandfold world system trembled, quaked, and shook; and an immeasurable, sublime radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the splendor of the devas.
Then the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance:
“Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!”
“Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!
Thus, this was how the Venerable Koṇḍañña came to be known by the name “Aññā-Koṇḍañña” (Koṇḍañña who has understood).
“‘This is the noble truth of suffering’: regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true insight arose, and light arose.”
“Vision arose”—
in what sense? “Knowledge arose”— in what sense?
In what sense?
"Wisdom arose"—
in what sense?
"Knowledge arose"—
in what sense?
"Light arose"— in that sense.
In what sense?
"The eye arose" means in the sense of seeing.
"Knowledge arose"—
in the sense of having been known. "Wisdom arose"— in the sense of having been understood.
In the sense of understanding.
"True knowledge arose"—
in the sense of penetration.
"Light arose"— in the sense of radiance.
The eye is a phenomenon (dhamma), knowledge is a phenomenon, wisdom is a phenomenon, true insight is a phenomenon, and light is a phenomenon.
These five phenomena are both the objects and the domain of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).
Whatever is its object is its domain;
whatever is its domain is its object.
Therefore it is said:
"Knowledge regarding phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
Its meaning is the sense of seeing, the sense of knowing, the sense of understanding, the sense of penetration, and the sense of illumination.
These five matters are both the objects and the domains of the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
Whatever are its objects are its domains;
whatever are its domains are its objects.
Therefore it is said:
“Knowledge regarding meanings is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
There are expressions of phrasing and etymology for the purpose of demonstrating five things; there are expressions of phrasing and etymology for the purpose of demonstrating five meanings.
These ten modes of expression are both the objects and the domain of the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
Whatever are its objects are its domain;
whatever are its domain are its objects.
Therefore it is said:
“Knowledge regarding linguistic expressions is the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (nirutti-patisambhidā).
There are knowledges regarding five phenomena, knowledges regarding five meanings, and knowledges regarding ten linguistic expressions.
These twenty kinds of knowledge are both the objects and the spheres of the analytical knowledge of ready wit.
Those which are its objects are its spheres;
those which are its spheres are its objects.
Therefore it is said:
“Knowledge regarding inspired responses is the analytical knowledge of inspired response.
“‘This Noble Truth of suffering is to be fully understood’ … [and so on] …”

The eye is a phenomenon (dhamma), knowledge is a phenomenon, wisdom is a phenomenon, true insight is a phenomenon, and light is a phenomenon.

The meaning of seeing is the meaning; the meaning of knowing is the meaning; the meaning of understanding is the meaning; the meaning of penetration is the meaning; the meaning of illumination is the meaning.

Whatever are its objects, those are its domains.
Whatever is its range is its object.
Therefore it is said:
"Knowledge regarding meanings is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā)."
The verbal expressions of phrasing and terminology used to point out five things, and the verbal expressions of phrasing and terminology used to point out five meanings—
these ten modes of expression are both the objects and the domain of the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
Whatever constitutes its objects, those constitute its domain.
Whatever is its range is its object.
Therefore it is called "the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), which is knowledge regarding linguistic expressions."
There are knowledges regarding five phenomena, knowledges regarding five meanings, and knowledges regarding ten linguistic expressions.
These twenty knowledges are both the objects and the spheres of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
Those which are its objects are its spheres.
Whatever are its objects are its cognitive bases.
Therefore it is called "the analytical knowledge of perspicuity regarding inspired speech."
Regarding the noble truth of suffering, there are fifteen phenomena, fifteen meanings, thirty modes of expression, and sixty types of knowledge.

In the four Noble Truths, there are sixty states, sixty meanings, one hundred and twenty expressions, and four hundred and forty-two kinds of knowledge. 2.6.2.

In the four bases for psychic power, there are sixty states, sixty meanings, one hundred and twenty modes of expression, and two hundred and forty kinds of knowledge.
2.6.4. The Chapter on the Seven Types of Bodhisattvas
“‘Origination, origination,’ monks, thus arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī, regarding things unheard of before, vision ...
[and so on] ... light.
‘Cessation, cessation,’ monks, thus arose in the Bodhisatta Vipassī, regarding things unheard of before, vision ... [and so on] ...”
“Light arose.
In the prophetic declaration of the Bodhisatta Vipassī, there were ten points, ten meanings, twenty modes of expression, and forty kinds of knowledge.
“‘The origin, the origin,’ monks, was the thought that arose in the Bodhisatta Sikhī... [and so on].
Of the Bodhisatta Vessabhu …pe… of the Bodhisatta Kakusandha …pe… of the Bodhisatta Koṇāgamana …pe…
To the Bodhisatta Kassapa, regarding things unheard of before, there arose the eye … [as before] … light arose:
“Cessation, cessation,” monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose the eye to the Bodhisatta Kassapa … [as before] … light arose.
“Light arose.
In the prophecy concerning the Bodhisatta Kassapa, there are ten phenomena, ten meanings, twenty linguistic expressions, and forty types of knowledge.
“‘Origination, origination,’ monks, regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in the Bodhisatta Gotama... [and so on]... light arose.”
“‘Cessation, cessation,’ monks, regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in the Bodhisatta Gotama; ...
light arose.”
In the declaration of the Bodhisatta Gotama, there are ten phenomena (*dhamma*), ten meanings (*attha*), twenty linguistic expressions (*nirutti*), and forty kinds of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
In the declarations of the seven Bodhisattas, there are seventy phenomena, seventy meanings, one hundred and forty linguistic expressions, and two hundred and eighty kinds of knowledge.
2.6.5. Section on Higher Knowledge (*Abhiññādivāra*)
“To the extent that the meaning of direct knowledge has been known, seen, understood, realized,
and touched with wisdom— there is no meaning of direct knowledge untouched by wisdom”—
thus the eye arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true insight arose, and light arose.
Regarding direct knowledge, there are twenty-five states of direct knowledge, twenty-five meanings, fifty modes of expression, and one hundred kinds of knowledge.
“To the extent that there is full understanding, there are [twenty-five] meanings of full understanding...
To the extent that there is abandoning, there are [twenty-five] meanings of abandoning... [and so on].
"Insofar as there is the meaning of development through development...
[and so on] ...insofar as there is the meaning of realization through realization, that has been known, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom.
There is no meaning of realization untouched by wisdom."
“Vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
Regarding the meaning of realization, there are twenty-five phenomena, twenty-five meanings, fifty modes of expression, and one hundred kinds of knowledge.
Regarding the meaning of direct higher knowledge, regarding the meaning of full understanding, regarding the meaning of abandoning, and regarding the meaning of development...
Regarding realization, there are one hundred and twenty-five states, one hundred and twenty-five meanings, two hundred and fifty etymological explanations, and five hundred kinds of knowledge.
2.6.6. Section on the Aggregates, etc.
“To the extent that the meaning of the aggregates as aggregates has been known, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom—
to the extent that there is no meaning of the aggregates as aggregates untouched by wisdom”—
thus did the eye arise, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true insight arose, and light arose.
Regarding the aggregates in the sense of the aggregate-meaning, there are twenty-five phenomena, twenty-five meanings, fifty designations, and one hundred kinds of knowledge.
“To whatever extent there is the element-meaning of the elements …pe… to whatever extent there is the base-meaning of the bases …pe…”

‘To whatever extent there is the meaning of the conditioned in conditioned things …pe… to whatever extent there is the meaning of the unconditioned in the unconditioned, that has been known, seen, understood, realized,
and touched with wisdom. There is no meaning of the unconditioned that has not been touched with wisdom.’”
“The eye arose … light arose. Regarding the unconditioned,
there are twenty-five states, twenty-five meanings, fifty expressions, and one hundred kinds of knowledge.
In the sense of aggregates among aggregates, in the sense of elements among elements, in the sense of bases among bases, in the sense of the conditioned among the conditioned,
and in the sense of the unconditioned among the unconditioned, there are one hundred and twenty-five states, one hundred and twenty-five meanings,
two hundred and fifty etymological explanations, and five hundred kinds of knowledge.
2.6.7. Chapter on Truths (Saccavāra) “To the extent that there is the meaning of suffering in suffering, it has been known, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom.
There is no meaning of suffering untouched by wisdom.”—thus it is said.
The eye arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true insight arose, light arose.
Regarding the meaning of suffering as suffering, there are twenty-five phenomena, twenty-five meanings, fifty modes of expression, and one hundred kinds of knowledge.
“To whatever extent there is the meaning of origin regarding the origin …” [and so forth].
To the extent that the meaning of cessation as cessation...
[and so on] ...to the extent that the meaning of the path as the path is known, seen, understood, realized,
and touched by wisdom— to that extent there is no meaning of the path untouched by wisdom.
“Vision arose … light arose. Regarding the path’s status as a path,
there are twenty-five phenomena, twenty-five meanings, fifty linguistic expressions, and one hundred types of knowledge.

In the four Noble Truths, there are one hundred phenomena (*dhamma*), one hundred meanings (*attha*), two hundred etymological explanations (*nirutti*), and four hundred kinds of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). 2.6.8.

Chapter on the Analytical Knowledges (*Paṭisambhidāvāra*) “To whatever extent there is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), its state as the analytical knowledge of meaning has been known, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom.”
‘The meaning of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) has not been touched by wisdom; the meaning of the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma does not exist’—
thus, the eye arose … pe … light arose.”
In the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), there are twenty-five states (dhamma), twenty-five meanings (attha), fifty expressions (nirutti), and one hundred knowledges (ñāṇa).

“To whatever extent there is the objective referent of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā) … [and so on] … to whatever extent there is the objective referent of the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā) …” [and so on].
"Insofar as the meaning of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity has been known, seen, understood, realized, and touched by wisdom through the analytical knowledge of perspicuity—
there is no meaning of the analytical knowledge of perspicuity that has not been touched by wisdom"—
thus the eye arose …pe….
“Light arose.
Regarding the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā): there are twenty-five phenomena, twenty-five meanings, fifty expressions, and one hundred knowledges.
Regarding the four analytical knowledges (catasso paṭisambhidā): there are one hundred phenomena, one hundred meanings, two hundred expressions, and four hundred knowledges.
2.6.9. The Chapter on the Dhamma of the Water-Buddha “To whatever extent there is knowledge of the degrees of the faculties—
whether it be known, seen, understood, realized, or touched by wisdom— to that extent there is no knowledge of the degrees of the faculties that is not touched by wisdom.”
“The eye arose … light arose. In the knowledge of the penetration of others’ faculties,
there are twenty-five phenomena, twenty-five meanings, fifty expressions, and one hundred knowledges.

“To the extent of the knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings …pe… to the extent of the knowledge of the Twin Miracle …pe… to the extent of the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion …pe…”
‘To the extent that there is omniscient knowledge …pe… to the extent that there is unobstructed knowledge, all that is known, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom;
there is no unobstructed knowledge not touched by wisdom.’”
“Vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true science arose, light arose.
In regard to unobstructed knowledge, there are twenty-five states, twenty-five meanings, fifty linguistic expressions, and one hundred kinds of knowledge.
In regard to the six qualities of a Buddha, there are one hundred and fifty states, one hundred and fifty meanings, three hundred linguistic expressions, and six hundred kinds of knowledge.

In the section on the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidādhikaraṇa*), there are eight hundred and fifty topics (*dhamma*), eight hundred and fifty meanings (*attha*), one thousand seven hundred etymologies (*nirutti*), three thousand four hundred knowledges (*ñāṇa*).
The Discourse on the Analytical Knowledges is concluded.
